clue.text: Imposing women arrange bets

parts.note: to do a room, or someone's hair, is to arrange it
a wager is a bet, the older and grander word for it

explanation.surface: Grand ladies organise a flutter on the horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imposing' looks like an instruction — to impose is to place one thing upon another — and it is nothing of the kind. It is half the definition, doing plain descriptive work.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowager is a widow who keeps her late husband's title, and the word carries exactly the grand, formidable bearing 'imposing' describes.

clue.text: Particular canine abandoned by waterway

indicators.note: To be abandoned by someone is to be left without them, so the longer word has to be read minus that letter.

parts.note: a canal is a waterway cut by hand rather than one a river made
a dentist marks the canine tooth C on a chart, and that C is what walks out

explanation.surface: A fussy dog is left behind on the canal towpath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canine' puts a dog on the towpath, which is the whole misdirection: it is the tooth, and the tooth is written as a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Anal' is short for anal-retentive, so it means obsessively fussy over detail — the pointed sense of 'particular' rather than the neutral one.

clue.text: Car rentals regularly in competition

indicators.note: the picked letters go inside the competition word

parts.note: a bee is a contest or gathering, as in a spelling bee

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals, here the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Car' is the Volkswagen Beetle. 'regularly' picks ETL from rentals, which goes 'in' BEE, as in a spelling bee.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beetle is the classic small Volkswagen model, so it is a make of car.

clue.text: Derisive remark about my Picasso?

indicators.note: A remark made about something goes round its subject, and these letters do the same — one word closes over the other.

parts.note: a jeer is a taunt shouted at somebody
'my!' and 'well!' are the same mild exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a painting the speaker hopes is a Picasso.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is somebody sneering at a painting, so Pablo is the Picasso you reach for. The clue wants his daughter, who works in a different material.
explanation.definitionFit: Paloma Picasso has designed jewellery for Tiffany for decades, so the surname names a trade through one practitioner — which the question mark admits.

clue.text: Fruit recipe stopping tennis ace going bananas

indicators.note: to stop something is to plug it, so the letter goes in as a stopper
going crazy, so the letters of tennis ace are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material
R is the abbreviation for recipe, from the Latin on prescriptions

explanation.surface: A tennis star loses it over a recipe for fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' tempts as the fruit, but 'going bananas' is the anagram signal: TENNIS ACE becomes NECTAINES, and R goes in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A nectarine is a smooth-skinned variety of peach, so it is a fruit.

clue.text: Top ambassador interrupting ball

indicators.note: An interruption breaks into something already under way, so these letters land in the middle of the word rather than after it.

parts.note: a bead is a small ball, the kind threaded on a string
an ambassador is His or Her Excellency, HE in diplomatic address

explanation.surface: A senior diplomat cuts in at a formal dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top ambassador' reads as one phrase about a senior diplomat. 'Top' is standing alone, and it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To top something is to cut its top off — the gardener's word and the executioner's — which is exactly the operation the answer names.

clue.text: Wrestler's trick with bad acne

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.walkthrough: John Cena is an American professional wrestler and actor. A john, like a trick, is slang for a prostitute's customer; 'bad' turns ACNE into CENA.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cena is a famous WWE professional wrestler, so the name answers 'Wrestler is'.

clue.text: Means business

definitions.meaning: the philosopher's sense: the capacity to act, the power by which a thing gets done
a firm that acts for its clients — an advertising one, an estate one, a recruitment one

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and no wordplay whatever. 'Means business' is an idiom about determination, and reading it as one phrase is exactly what stops you splitting it.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the power to act, the means by which something happens; the other is the firm that acts on a client's behalf.

clue.text: Small opening in Gogglebox you once rejected

indicators.note: To reject something is to throw it back, and a word thrown back is read the other way round.

parts.note: the gogglebox is British slang for the television set, the tele
'ye' is the old form of 'you', the one Chaucer's readers used

explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Gogglebox the television programme, people filmed watching television, while the letters need the older slang for the set in the corner.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyelet is the small ringed hole punched in a shoe or a sail for a lace or a rope to pass through.

clue.text: Sample from Lulu apparently repulsed my colleague

indicators.note: A sample is a piece taken out of something larger, so the letters are lifted from within the words that follow.
To repulse is to drive back, so the letters picked out run in the opposite direction.

parts.note: four consecutive letters straddling the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A snippet sampled from a Lulu record reportedly disgusted a workmate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sample from Lulu' reads as a record credit, which is where the eye goes. 'My colleague' means a fellow Guardian setter, so the definition wants a person rather than a job.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul is one of the Guardian's regular cryptic setters, so 'my colleague' identifies the answer as a name on the same rota as Brockwell.

clue.text: Musicians performing late in ancient city

indicators.note: 'in' is doing literal work: the rearranged letters go inside the city's name, not beside it.

parts.note: Thebes, the great city of ancient Egypt on the Nile

parts.note: the four letters of LATE, shuffled before they go in

explanation.surface: A band plays a late-night gig among the ruins of an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musicians performing late' is a complete picture of a band on after midnight, and every word of it turns out to be doing a different job.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Musicians' is a plain category label, and the plural covers a four-man group whose name carries its own definite article.

clue.text: Stuff clinging to the back of Pete Best?

indicators.note: Something clinging to an object has its arms all the way round it, so one word closes over the letter that follows.

parts.note: to stuff yourself and to gorge are the same greedy verb

parts.note: only its final letter is used

explanation.surface: Something sticky has got stuck to the back of Pete Best, the Beatles' original drummer.
explanation.walkthrough: Pete Best reads as one name, the drummer the band let go, and the clue takes him apart: Pete supplies a letter, and Best is the definition — George Best the footballer.
explanation.definitionFit: George Best was Manchester United's Northern Irish winger, so 'Best?' reaches a first name through one famous bearer of the surname.

clue.text: One who may charge money around statue

parts.note: rhino is old British slang for cash
c. for circa, the letter written in front of an approximate date
the winged archer above Piccadilly Circus, London's best-known statue

explanation.surface: Someone who might charge for their services hangs about near a statue with the cash.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is 'around': it looks like an instruction to wrap one piece about another, and it pays out a single letter instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhinoceros charges — lowers its horn and runs at you — while the billing sense of 'charge' belongs entirely to the surface.

clue.text: Militant going into business with John Denver here

a rad is a radical, someone at the militant end of a cause

explanation.surface: An activist goes into business with the singer John Denver in his home state.
explanation.walkthrough: John Denver reads as one name, and the clue takes it in two: the first half is bathroom slang, and only the second half is defining anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Denver is Colorado's capital, so 'Denver here' asks for the state that city stands in — a place named by what it contains.

clue.text: Ducks once more coming back for rest

indicators.note: Something coming back retraces its path, and in an across entry that means reading the letters from the right.

parts.note: to duck is to dip, and the re- on the front is 'once more'

explanation.surface: Ducks dive under again before coming back to the bank to rest.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker a spider is the arched rest you stand over the ball for a shot you cannot stretch to, so 'rest' is the table's word and not the sofa's.
explanation.definitionFit: A spider is the long-legged cue rest that arches above a ball in snooker, so 'rest' is being used in its billiard-hall sense.

clue.text: 3 characters in hotel ate ridiculously

indicators.note: Characters are letters, and the ones wanted are those standing inside the words that follow.

parts.note: eight unbroken letters running across all three words, starting inside the first

explanation.surface: Three guests in a hotel ate an absurd amount.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ridiculously' reads as an anagram signal, and that is the trap — it is there to finish the run of letters. The definition is the number, pointing at another entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An elaterid is a click beetle, the family that snaps itself upright when flipped, so it is one instance of what 3 down spells.

clue.text: German band love Foreigner, but not in a nice way

definitions.text: Foreigner, but not in a nice way

a band is a ring — the thing on a finger, not the group on stage

explanation.definitionFit: Gringo is what Spanish-speaking Latin America calls an English-speaking outsider, and it is rarely a compliment — which the definition's second half owns up to.

clue.text: Islander's fine home about to get washed out

parts.note: fine and OK are the same shrug of approval

explanation.definitionFit: An Okinawan is a person from Okinawa, so the definition is the plain -an form English builds for the inhabitant of a place.

the latest letter is the last one

clue.text: Child cuddling cross monster

clue.text: Every year songbirds going west over the hill

clue.text: Long track in evergreen forest

clue.text: Number 19 nailing 501
